patch_description:
Crossover of the two best-performing seeds. The winning seed (score 0.60)
showed that collapsing the circuit down to very few distinct trainable
parameter names — one global RY angle, one global RZ angle, and one shared
entangling angle spread across multiple connectivity "shells" (nearest,
skip-2, and antipodal) — beats architectures with more per-qubit or
per-edge-type parameters, even though those have nominally higher
expressivity. The other seed contributed the idea of tying entangling gates
to the *same generator family* as a nearby single-qubit rotation (RZ pairs
naturally with CRZ, since CRZ is literally a controlled version of the RZ
generator), which lets us merge the single dedicated "entangling" parameter
into the RZ parameter itself without discarding the multi-shell connectivity
graph that made the winning seed effective.

Concretely, this candidate keeps:
  - a global RY layer (one shared parameter "theta_ry"), giving every qubit
    the same local rotation, exactly as in the winning seed;
  - a global RZ layer (one shared parameter "theta_z");
  - three CRZ entangling shells (distance-1 ring, distance-2 ring, and
    distance-4 antipodal pairing) that reuse the SAME "theta_z" parameter
    instead of introducing a third parameter name.

This reduces the circuit to only 2 distinct trainable parameter names (4
total with gain/bias), down from 3 in the best prior seed and 5 in the
weaker one. Per the stated scoring rule, fewer distinct parameter names
strictly improves the score, and reusing RZ's generator for the entanglers
is the most structurally justified way to remove a parameter without
deleting any gates or connectivity, preserving the multi-shell entangling
graph (and hence the expressivity/robustness) that made the 3-parameter
seed outperform the 5-parameter one. Repeating this block 3 times with tied
parameters (as fixed by the harness) still yields a non-trivial, richly
connected circuit (36 gates/block, 108 gates total) while asking the
optimizer to fit only 2 circuit angles, which should shrink the
train-validation-test gap and speed up convergence on the small training
set.
